731	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{RP Prec} & \textbf{Text Prec} & $\Delta$\textbf{Prec} & $\Delta$\textbf{BA} \\
732	\midrule
733	R1-8B & .621 & .416 & +.205 & +.140 \\
734	OT-7B & .371 & .244 & +.127 & +.128 \\
735	QwQ-32B & .563 & .391 & +.172 & +.132 \\
736	R1-32B & .524 & .441 & +.083 & +.085 \\
737	\bottomrule
738	\end{tabular}
739	\end{table}
740	
741	All four models retain significant HS advantage under random projection ($\Delta$Prec +8.3 to +20.5pp), with cross-seed standard deviations below 1.7pp. RP precision is slightly lower than PCA-384d (expected, as PCA preserves maximal variance), but the gap is small. The small gap weakens a pure capacity explanation: even a structure-destroying projection preserves the HS advantage. The safety signal appears broadly distributed across hidden-state dimensions rather than concentrated in top principal components.
742	
743	
744	\section{LLM-Based Text Encoder Comparison}
745	\label{app:e5_mistral}
746	
747	To test whether an LLM-based text encoder closes the HS advantage gap, we encode each reasoning step with E5-Mistral-7B-Instruct~\citep{wang2024e5mistral} (4096d, reduced to 384d via PCA to match the MiniLM dimensionality). \cref{tab:e5_mistral} reports precision comparisons against HS probes at threshold-based layers.
748	
749	\begin{table}[h]
750	\centering
751	\small
752	\caption{HS vs.\ E5-Mistral-7B (PCA 384d) precision. HB: Holm-Bonferroni adjusted (4 tests, $\alpha{=}0.05$). MiniLM precision from \cref{tab:hs_vs_text} for reference. 60/20/20 split.}
753	\label{tab:e5_mistral}
754	\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
755	\toprule
756	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Layer} & $W$ & \textbf{HS} & \textbf{E5} & \textbf{MiniLM} & $\Delta$(HS$-$E5) & $p$ & \textbf{HB} \\
757	\midrule
758	R1-8B & L14 & 3 & .630 & .480 & .416 & +15.0 & 0.001 & \checkmark \\
759	OT-7B & L16 & 3 & .446 & .321 & .244 & +12.5 & 0.009 & \checkmark \\
760	R1-32B & L63 & 1 & .588 & .506 & .441 & +8.2 & 0.235 & \\
761	QwQ-32B & L63 & 5 & .515 & .447 & .391 & +6.8 & 0.368 & \\
762	\bottomrule
763	\end{tabular}
764	\end{table}
765	
766	The HS advantage partially survives against the LLM encoder: 2/4 models (both 7--8B) retain significance after Holm-Bonferroni correction. Three text encoders form a monotonic gradient: MiniLM (22M params, 384d): 4/4 HB; E5-Mistral (7B, PCA 384d): 2/4 HB; BGE-large (335M, 1024d): 1/4 HB (\cref{app:encoder_robustness}). E5 precision consistently falls between MiniLM and HS across all models, consistent with encoder quality progressively narrowing the gap. PCA to 384d discards information from the 4096d E5 representation; the comparison controls dimensionality but not representation quality, so the true E5 advantage may be larger than reported here.
767	
768	
769	\section{Position-Residualized Probing}
770	\label{app:position_residual}
771	
772	To quantify non-positional safety signal, we regress out the normalized position $t/T$ from each hidden-state (or text-embedding) vector before training the logistic regression probe. \cref{tab:position_residual} summarizes results across all models at their optimal $W$.
773	
774	\begin{table}[h]
775	\centering
776	\small
777	\begin{tabular}{lcrrrr}
778	\toprule
779	\textbf{Model} & $W$ & \textbf{HS BA} & \textbf{Resid.\ HS BA} & \textbf{Drop} & \textbf{Resid.\ Text BA} \\
780	\midrule
781	R1-8B & 15 & 0.834 & 0.669 & 16.5pp & 0.605 \\
782	R1-8B & 3 & 0.813 & 0.571 & 24.3pp & 0.534 \\
783	OT-7B & 3 & 0.732 & 0.609 & 12.3pp & 0.540 \\
784	QwQ-32B & 3 & 0.796 & 0.619 & 17.7pp & 0.582 \\
785	R1-32B & 1 & 0.756 & 0.552 & 20.4pp & 0.532 \\
786	\bottomrule
787	\end{tabular}
788	\caption{Position-residualized probe balanced accuracy. All residualized HS probes are above chance ($p{<}0.001$). 3/4 models retain significant non-positional HS advantage over text (gap +3.7 to +6.9pp, HB corrected); R1-32B is the exception (+1.9pp, $p{=}0.914$).}
789	\label{tab:position_residual}
790	\end{table}
791	
792	Position accounts for 9--20pp of balanced accuracy depending on model and window size (R1-32B's 20.4pp drop at $W{=}1$ reflects the absence of temporal context), and all models retain non-positional signal above chance ($p{<}0.001$). Three of four models retain significant non-positional HS advantage over text after residualization (OT-7B +6.9pp, R1-8B +6.4pp at $W{=}15$, QwQ-32B +3.7pp; all HB corrected). R1-32B is the exception: residualized HS-text gap is +1.9pp ($p{=}0.914$), so its HS advantage is position-mediated. Larger temporal windows reduce position dependence: R1-8B drops 24.3pp at $W{=}3$ but only 16.5pp at $W{=}15$.
793	
794	For QwQ-32B specifically, three complementary significance tests confirm the residualized probe performs above chance: Wilcoxon signed-rank $p{=}0.0024$, paired $t$-test $p{=}0.0008$, permutation test $p{<}0.001$ (bootstrap 95\% CI for per-trace BA: $[0.575, 0.744]$). The position baseline achieves higher balanced accuracy (0.832 vs.\ HS 0.796), and HS precision (+4.5pp, $p{=}0.133$) and FPR (+2.5pp, $p{=}0.279$) margins over the position baseline are not statistically significant at $n{=}19$.
795	
796	
797	\section{Hyperparameter Robustness}
798	\label{app:hyperparameter_robustness}
799	
800	The joint search space for layer (${\leq}64$), window $W$ (7 values), consecutive-crossing threshold $K$ (5 values), and decision threshold is large (up to 2{,}240 configurations per model). This raises the concern that reported performance reflects overfitting to small validation sets ($n{=}4$--$9$ per class at 32B). Three analyses address this concern.
801	
802	\paragraph{Threshold-based metrics converge to a deep-layer band.}
803	Despite the large search space, three of four threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) independently select L63 (98\% depth) for both 32B models (\cref{tab:layer_selection}). A joint (layer, $W$) grid search over 192 configurations confirms that L63 is near-optimal for QwQ-32B at recommended windows (\cref{tab:joint_layer_w}). For R1-32B, layers L55--L63 at $W{=}1$ form a robust band where all 3/3 metrics pass Holm-Bonferroni (\cref{app:layer_sweep}). The convergence of independent metrics to a narrow band is inconsistent with overfitting, which would produce scattered selections.
804	
805	\paragraph{BA-optimal layer instability is the finding, not a confound.}
806	Five-fold cross-validation on 32B validation sets reveals that balanced-accuracy-optimal layers are highly unstable across folds (\cref{tab:fold_ba_layers}). This instability is not a limitation of the study but the central methodological finding: BA-layer selection is sensitive to data composition, and conclusions drawn from any single BA-optimal layer are unreliable. Despite per-fold instability, mean BA across folds peaks near L47--L50 for both models, consistent with the LOO-CV dominant layers (\cref{app:layer_sweep}). The HS advantage holds at both BA-optimal and precision-optimal layers regardless of depth (14/16 per-model tests pass HB; \cref{tab:ba_layer_comparison}).
807	
808	\begin{table}[h]
809	\centering
810	\small
811	\caption{BA-optimal layer per fold (5-fold CV, 32B models). Per-fold selections span 24 layers, but mean-BA landscape peaks are stable.}
812	\label{tab:fold_ba_layers}
813	\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}
814	\toprule
815	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{F2} & \textbf{F3} & \textbf{F4} & \textbf{F5} & \textbf{Spread} & \textbf{Mean-BA best} \\
816	\midrule
817	QwQ-32B & L63 & L51 & L39 & L44 & L44 & 24 layers & L50 \\
818	R1-32B & L53 & L45 & L40 & L63 & L39 & 24 layers & L47 \\
819	\bottomrule
820	\end{tabular}
821	\end{table}
822	
823	\paragraph{Bootstrap CIs quantify statistical uncertainty.}
824	For the most fragile result (R1-8B FPR), bias-corrected accelerated (BCa) bootstrap~\citep{efron1993bootstrap} yields a 95\% CI of [0.006, 0.159] ($p{=}0.033$), with 12\% leave-one-out instability (\cref{app:multi_seed}). The CI excludes zero and confirms significance despite seed fragility. CP annotation perturbation (\cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) further shows that $\pm 2$-step label noise changes BA by ${<}2.5$pp, so annotation uncertainty does not compound with hyperparameter selection.
825	
826	\subsection{Nested Cross-Validation}
827	\label{app:nested_cv}
828	
829	The holdout estimates in \cref{tab:hs_vs_text} select layer and window on the validation fold, then evaluate on a fixed test set. To rule out hyperparameter overfitting, we run nested 5-fold cross-validation on both 7--8B models: the outer fold holds out test data; the inner loop selects (layer, $W$) on the remaining four folds. \cref{tab:nested_cv} reports per-fold precision differences.
830	
831	\begin{table}[h]
832	\centering
833	\small
834	\caption{Nested 5-fold CV: per-fold HS$-$text precision difference (pp). Layer and $W$ selected independently per fold. All 10/10 folds favor HS.}
835	\label{tab:nested_cv}
836	\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
837	\begin{tabular}{lcccccccc}
838	\toprule
839	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{F2} & \textbf{F3} & \textbf{F4} & \textbf{F5} & \textbf{Mean} & \textbf{Holdout} & \textbf{Shrink.} \\
840	\midrule
841	R1-8B & +22.1 & +14.4 & +17.5 & +17.0 & +16.0 & $+17.4 \pm 2.6$ & +20.1 & 13\% \\
842	OT-7B & +13.2 & +21.4 & +18.8 & +12.6 & +15.8 & $+16.4 \pm 3.3$ & +21.9 & 25\% \\
843	\bottomrule
844	\end{tabular}
845	\begin{flushleft}
846	\scriptsize R1-8B selected layers: L12, L12, L12, L13, L14; $W_\text{HS}$: 3, 3, 5, 5, 3. OT-7B selected layers: L23, L21, L27, L26, L26 (75--96\% depth); $W_\text{HS}$: 5, 5, 5, 5, 5.
847	\end{flushleft}
848	\end{table}
849	
850	The HS precision advantage is consistent across all 10 folds (5/5 for each model), with mean advantages of +17.4pp (R1-8B) and +16.4pp (OT-7B). Shrinkage relative to holdout estimates is 13\% and 25\% respectively, within expected ranges for validation-selected hyperparameters. R1-8B layer selection is stable (L12--L14, 38--44\% depth), consistent with all five metrics agreeing on L14 in the main analysis. OT-7B nested CV selects L21--L27 (75--96\% depth), deeper than the CR-composite-selected L16 (57\%) used in the main text. The discrepancy between CR-composite-selected (L16) and precision-selected (L21--L27) layers further illustrates the metric-dependence of layer selection documented in \cref{sec:layer-results}.
851	
852	
853	\section{Multi-Seed Stability}
854	\label{app:multi_seed}
855	
856	\cref{tab:multi_seed} reports LR probe performance across 5 random seeds at each model's threshold-based layer and optimal $W$.
857	
858	\begin{table}[h]
859	\centering
860	\small
861	\caption{LR probe stability across 5 random seeds (threshold-based layers, optimal $W$). 7--8B models are stable; R1-32B shows high variance due to small sample ($n{=}20$).}
862	\label{tab:multi_seed}
863	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
864	\toprule
865	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Precision} & \textbf{Bal.\ Acc} & \textbf{FPR} \\
866	\midrule
867	R1-8B & $0.590 \pm 0.072$ & $0.756 \pm 0.028$ & $0.154 \pm 0.026$ \\
868	OT-7B & $0.421 \pm 0.034$ & $0.633 \pm 0.023$ & $0.157 \pm 0.021$ \\
869	QwQ-32B & $0.651 \pm 0.099$ & $0.731 \pm 0.028$ & $0.133 \pm 0.032$ \\
870	R1-32B & $0.594 \pm 0.128$ & $0.692 \pm 0.056$ & $0.207 \pm 0.145$ \\
871	\bottomrule
872	\end{tabular}
873	\end{table}
874	
875	R1-32B's high FPR variance (std $= 0.145$) reflects a single outlier seed (FPR $= 0.48$), amplified by the small test set ($n{=}20$). Note that R1-32B's absolute precision std (12.8pp) differs markedly from its paired $\Delta$Prec std (2.0pp): HS and text precision covary across seeds.
876	
877	\paragraph{5-seed Holm-Bonferroni pass rates.} \cref{tab:seed_hb} reports HB pass rates per model across 5 seeds. Overall, 18/20 (90\%) model-seed combinations pass full HB (3/3 metrics).
878	
879	\begin{table}[h]
880	\centering
881	\small
882	\caption{5-seed HB pass rates (3/3 metrics per seed). R1-8B failures are FPR-specific.}
883	\label{tab:seed_hb}
884	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
885	\toprule
886	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{HB Pass} & \textbf{Mean $\Delta$Prec $\pm$ std} & \textbf{Note} \\
887	\midrule
888	OT-7B & 5/5 & $+20.9 \pm 1.3$pp & Cleanest evidence \\
889	R1-32B & 5/5 & $+13.7 \pm 2.0$pp & Position-mediated \\
890	QwQ-32B & 5/5 & $+19.9 \pm 2.5$pp & Robust \\
891	R1-8B & 3/5 & $+14.6 \pm 4.5$pp & FPR seed-fragile \\
892	\bottomrule
893	\end{tabular}
894	\end{table}
895	
896	\paragraph{R1-8B FPR per-seed breakdown.} \cref{tab:r18b_fpr_seeds} reports per-seed HS vs.\ text FPR comparisons for R1-8B. The HS advantage is directionally consistent (5/5 seeds), with 2/5 reaching $p{<}0.05$ uncorrected; after Bonferroni correction for 5 seeds ($\alpha{=}0.01$), 1/5 remains significant. Text FPR is highly stable (std $= 0.007$) while HS FPR is split-sensitive (std $= 0.040$), which explains why the canonical-split FPR advantage ($-7.4$pp) does not generalize robustly across seeds.
897	
898	\begin{table}[h]
899	\centering
900	\small
901	\caption{R1-8B FPR per-seed comparison (L14, $W{=}15$; main text \cref{tab:hs_vs_text} reports $W{=}3$ after 5-seed validation). Direction is consistent (5/5 HS $\leq$ Text); 2/5 reach $p{<}0.05$ uncorrected, 1/5 after Bonferroni correction (5 seeds, $\alpha{=}0.01$).}
902	\label{tab:r18b_fpr_seeds}
903	\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
904	\toprule
905	\textbf{Seed} & \textbf{HS FPR} & \textbf{Text FPR} & $\Delta$\textbf{FPR} & $p$ \\
906	\midrule
907	0 & 0.161 & 0.165 & $-$0.004 & 0.440 \\
908	1 & 0.061 & 0.166 & $-$0.105 & ${<}0.001$ \\
909	2 & 0.123 & 0.176 & $-$0.053 & 0.093 \\
910	3 & 0.148 & 0.167 & $-$0.018 & 0.293 \\

915	\end{tabular}
916	\end{table}
917	
918	\paragraph{R1-8B per-metric HB pass rates.} \cref{tab:r18b_metric_hb} reports Holm-Bonferroni pass rates per metric across 5 seeds for R1-8B, the model classified as ``moderate'' evidence due to FPR instability.
919	
920	\begin{table}[h]
921	\centering
922	\small
923	\caption{R1-8B per-metric$\times$seed HB pass rates. Precision is robust (5/5); FPR is fragile (3/5). FPR std across seeds is 0.040 vs.\ text FPR std 0.007, consistent with a proportion near boundary (${\sim}$12\%) amplified at $n{=}43$.}
924	\label{tab:r18b_metric_hb}
925	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
926	\toprule
927	\textbf{Seed} & $\Delta$\textbf{Prec HB} & $\Delta$\textbf{BA HB} & $\Delta$\textbf{FPR HB} \\
928	\midrule

940	The FPR instability has a clear source: R1-8B text FPR clusters tightly around 17\% (std${=}0.7$pp) while HS FPR ranges from 6.1\% to 16.1\% (std${=}4.0$pp). Seeds where HS FPR happens to be high ($>$14\%) lose significance because the gap against text narrows below the detection threshold at $n{=}43$. This instability is metric-specific and does not affect the precision or balanced accuracy advantage, which passes all 5 seeds.
941	
942	\paragraph{R1-32B per-seed breakdown.} \cref{tab:r132b_seeds} reports the full per-seed breakdown for R1-32B. Seed 0 is an outlier (FPR $= 0.483$), driven by test-set trace allocation at $n{=}20$. Excluding seed 0, FPR std drops from 0.145 to 0.046.

945	\centering
946	\small

948	\label{tab:r132b_seeds}
949	\begin{tabular}{cccc}
950	\toprule
951	\textbf{Seed} & \textbf{Precision} & \textbf{Bal.\ Acc} & \textbf{FPR} \\
952	\midrule
953	0 & 0.441 & 0.594 & 0.483 \\
954	1 & 0.750 & 0.748 & 0.109 \\
955	2 & 0.685 & 0.670 & 0.111 \\

957	4 & 0.444 & 0.715 & 0.221 \\
958	\midrule
959	mean$\pm$std & $0.594 \pm 0.128$ & $0.692 \pm 0.056$ & $0.207 \pm 0.145$ \\
960	\bottomrule
961	\end{tabular}
962	\end{table}
963	
964	
965	\section{BA-Layer Modality Comparison}
966	\label{tab:ba_layer_comparison}
967	
968	To address the concern that threshold-based layer selection may circularly favor HS probes, we repeat the modality comparison at layers selected by pure balanced accuracy, a threshold-free metric (\cref{tab:ba_layer_results}). BA-optimal layers vary widely across models (7--98\% depth), itself demonstrating that layer selection is a consequential methodological choice. The HS advantage is significant at whichever layer BA selects (14/16 per-model HB, two FPR failures from underpowered 32B test sets $n{\leq}20$).
969	
970	\begin{table}[h]
971	\centering
972	\small
973	\caption{HS vs.\ text at BA-selected layers (60/20/20 split, same as main results). 14/16 per-model tests pass Holm-Bonferroni ($\alpha{=}0.05$); two FPR failures from underpowered 32B sets. BA-L: layer selected by pure balanced accuracy. Depth varies from 7\% to 98\%.}
974	\label{tab:ba_layer_results}
975	\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
976	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
977	\toprule
978	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{BA-L} & $\Delta$\textbf{Prec} & $\Delta$\textbf{BA} & $\Delta$\textbf{FPR} & $\Delta$\textbf{AUROC} \\
979	\midrule
980	R1-8B & L17 & +18.6 ({<}.001) & +8.4 (.006) & $-$7.0 (.043) & +12.1 (.009) \\
981	OT-7B & L2 & +18.5 ({<}.001) & +8.0 (.006) & $-$13.3 ({<}.001) & +12.8 (.003) \\
982	QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ & L63 & +18.1 (.001) & +13.5 ({<}.001) & $-$6.4 (.088) & +15.1 (.001) \\
983	R1-32B$^\dagger$ & L46 & +12.8 (.014) & +17.6 ({<}.001) & $-$12.2 (.083) & +15.1 (.009) \\
984	\bottomrule
985	\end{tabular}
986	\begin{flushleft}
987	\scriptsize Values: difference in pp ($p$-value, bootstrap, 10{,}000 resamples). $\dagger$\,Sample-limited ($n \leq 20$).
988	\end{flushleft}
989	\end{table}
990	
991	Of 16 per-model tests (4 models $\times$ 4 metrics), 14 pass Holm-Bonferroni correction. The precision gains (+12.8 to +18.6pp) are comparable to those at threshold-based layers (+15.4 to +21.9pp; \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}), so the HS advantage is robust to the choice of layer selection criterion. The two failures are both FPR at 32B: R1-32B ($p{=}0.083$) and QwQ-32B ($p{=}0.088$), consistent with the underpowered test sets ($n{\leq}20$) noted throughout. BA-optimal depths span 7\% (OT-7B L2) to 98\% (QwQ-32B L63), in contrast to threshold-based layers that consistently select deep layers (94--98\%). That BA selection produces such depth variation while preserving significant HS advantage reinforces the core methodological finding: the advantage is genuine rather than an artifact of any particular layer selection criterion.
992	
993	
994	\section{Post-Hoc Power Analysis}
995	\label{app:power_analysis}
996	
997	We compute post-hoc minimum detectable effects (MDEs) at 80\% power for each model's test set to contextualize non-significant results, particularly at 32B scale where sample sizes are small (\cref{tab:power_analysis}).
998

I need: (1) the Soundness score scale and what each level means, (2) the Excitement score scale and what each level means, (3) the Overall Assessment score scale and what each level means, (4) the Confidence score scale. # ARR Review Scoring Scales

Based on my review of the ARR Reviewer Guidelines document, I must report that **the specific numeric scoring scales and their detailed definitions are not explicitly provided in this text**.

## What the Guidelines Actually Specify

The document mentions three score types introduced in February 2025:

1. **Soundness** - described as requiring justification by review text; "low Soundness scores without sufficient justification" are flagged as problematic
2. **Excitement** - characterized as "more subjective" and "orthogonal to the assessment of soundness"
3. **Overall Assessment** - presented as "a composite score reflecting soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact"

However, the guidelines do **not list the numeric ranges** (e.g., 1-5, 1-10) or provide definitions for each level (e.g., "5 = Excellent").

## Confidence Score

The document references a "confidence score" that reviewers can indicate but provides no scoring scale details.

## Recommendation

To obtain the actual numeric scales and level definitions, you would need to consult the detailed **ARR review form documentation** referenced in the guidelines, which is described separately at the ARR website.

Based on the search results, I found information about the ACL ARR 2025 review form. Here are the key details:

## Three Scoring Categories

Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation.

## Soundness Score

Soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review. If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it.

## Excitement Score

Subjective preferences should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons.

## Overall Assessment Score

The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact.

## Scale Details

The review form indicates a 5-point scale where 5 = Excellent, 4 = Strong, and 3 = Acceptable, though the search results show scores can also include decimals (like 2.5) based on reviewer discussions.

# ACL Rolling Review Form - Complete Scoring Dimensions

## Scored Fields

### Reviewer Confidence
*   5 = Positive evaluation is correct; read carefully, familiar with related work
*   4 = Quite sure; checked important points carefully
*   3 = Pretty sure; good general knowledge but didn't verify all details
*   2 = Willing to defend, but likely missed some details or novelty assessment
*   1 = Outside expertise area or paper very difficult to understand

### Soundness
*   5 = Excellent: Among the most thorough studies of its type
*   4.5
*   4 = Strong: Sufficient support for claims; minor extra experiments optional
*   3.5
*   3 = Acceptable: Main claims adequately supported with minor gaps
*   2.5
*   2 = Poor: Main claims lack sufficient support; major technical issues
*   1.5
*   1 = Major Issues: Insufficiently thorough or not relevant to ACL

### Excitement
*   5 = Highly Exciting: Would recommend to others; attend presentation
*   4.5
*   4 = Exciting: Mention to others; make effort to attend
*   3.5
*   3 = Interesting: Might mention points; attend if time permits
*   2.5
*   2 = Potentially Interesting: Doesn't resonate with reviewer but might with community
*   1.5
*   1 = Not Exciting: Doesn't resonate; unlikely to resonate with others

### Overall Assessment
*   5 = Consider for Award: Top 2.5% outstanding paper contender
*   4.5 = Borderline Award
*   4 = Conference: Acceptable for publication
*   3.5 = Borderline Conference
*   3 = Findings: Acceptable for Findings track
*   2.5 = Borderline Findings
*   2 = Resubmit next cycle: Needs substantial revisions
*   1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle: Needs extensive revisions
*   1 = Do not resubmit: Requires complete rework or irrelevant to ACL

### Reproducibility
*   5 = Results easily reproducible
*   4 = Mostly reproducible; minor variation possible
*   3 = Reproducible with difficulty; underspecified parameters
*   2 = Hard to reproduce; unavailable data or insufficient details
*   1 = Impossible to reproduce

### Datasets Value
*   5 = Enabling: Should affect research project choices
*   4 = Useful: Recommended for ongoing work
*   3 = Potentially useful: May benefit some research
*   2 = Documentary: Useful for replication only
*   1 = No usable datasets submitted

### Software Value
*   5 = Enabling: Should affect project choices
*   4 = Useful: Recommended to others
*   3 = Potentially useful: May benefit some work
*   2 = Documentary: Useful for replication only
*   1 = No usable software released

### Author Identity Knowledge
*   5 = Know/guess author name from submission violation
*   4 = Know/guess from preprint or workshop paper
*   3 = Know/guess from submission contents
*   2 = Know/guess from social media or talks
*   1 = No educated guess about identity

## Non-Scored Sections

- Paper Summary
- Summary of Strengths
- Summary of Weaknesses
- Comments/Suggestions/Typos
- Best paper justification (if award consideration)
- Limitations and Societal Impact
- Ethical Concerns
- Needs Ethics Review
- Conjecture as to author identity (optional)

content.thinking:
Now I have all the information I need to complete a thorough review. Let me compile my review focusing on the methodological rigor, statistical methods, and experimental design as instructed.

Let me organize my thoughts on the key issues:

**Statistical Methods:**

1. **Holm-Bonferroni correction framework**: The paper uses 12-test HB (3 metrics × 4 models) but argues the effective number is 4 (one per model) because BA, precision, FPR share a confusion matrix. This is reasonable but the argument needs scrutiny. The 3 metrics sharing a confusion matrix with 2 degrees of freedom means they are positively correlated, so HB is conservative. 

The critical concern is that the weakest test (R1-8B FPR, rank 12, p=0.044) barely clears the 12-test threshold of 0.050, and the paper claims identical conclusions under both frameworks, which is marginal given how close this result sits to significance.

2. **BCa bootstrap at n=19-20**: BCa bootstrap with these sample sizes is unreliable since estimating acceleration and bias parameters becomes unstable. The paper acknowledges this limitation and appropriately relies on exact permutation tests as the primary inference method for the 32B model instead.

3. **Exact permutation test**: The sign-flip permutation tests enumerate all 2^n possibilities, which is the gold standard for small samples, and they confirm all 6 of the 32B tests. This is methodologically sound.

4. **Multiple comparison correction and metric correlation**: The paper's argument that BA, precision, and FPR share a confusion matrix and therefore 12 tests overcorrects is theoretically valid, though the practical difference is negligible since both correction schemes reach the same conclusions.

**Experimental Design:**

The hyperparameter search space relative to sample size is a major concern. With 32B models having n=100 total, n=20 test, and only n=4-10 per-class validation, but searching across 64 layers × 7 W values × 5 K values × threshold—potentially 2,240 configurations—there's substantial overfitting risk.

The paper mitigates this through convergence analysis, nested CV, and multi-seed stability checks in the appendix, though nested CV wasn't applied to the 32B models. Leave-one-out cross-validation on the validation set reveals only 65-68% agreement on the dominant layer, suggesting the selection is unstable, and while the paper acknowledges this limitation, the framing could be more cautious about the implications.

There's also an inconsistency around K selection: the paper states K was set as a design choice before evaluation, but then describes it as selected on the R1-8B validation set to balance coverage and false positive rate, which contradicts the earlier claim.

The K ablation study does show the conclusions hold across K=3, 5, and 7, which provides some reassurance. However, the LOO-CV analysis was only performed on 7-8B models with nested cross-validation, while 32B models lack this rigorous overfitting check. Additionally, the GRU experiments use a different 70/30 data split compared to the main 60/20/20 protocol, making direct comparison less straightforward.

With only 95-100 traces total, the validation sets contain just 19-20 traces with 4-10 per class—far too small for reliably selecting among 2,240 configurations. The layer selection methodology also raises concerns: the paper defines CR-composite and threshold-based metrics post-hoc as an empirical observation, then uses this classification to support claims, which creates circularity. The paper acknowledges this but argues the ablation results are reproducible facts independent of the framing, and the random-CP control provides independent evidence supporting the findings.

The real risk is that by testing enough metrics, you'll find one that validates your preferred result. The paper's defense is solid though—three independent threshold-based metrics converge, the random-CP control shows the shallow-layer bias is geometric rather than from data snooping, cosine compression is independently verifiable, and nested CV confirms the advantage. Still, the paper could be clearer about distinguishing discovery from confirmation. On OT-7B specifically, CR-composite selects L0 while threshold-based selects L16, showing how dramatically these approaches diverge.

The layer selection varies substantially across metrics and folds, which is actually the paper's main point about sensitivity, but it also means the reported results hinge on which layer they ended up using. For the control task, selectivity sits at 11.1-16.8 percentage points above chance while position contributes 9-20 percentage points—there's real overlap here, though the paper is transparent about it. R1-32B's residualized selectivity drops to just 3.0 percentage points, below their 5 percentage point threshold, which they properly acknowledge. The residualized gap for R1-32B is only 1.9 percentage points with p=0.914, and they correctly flag this as exploratory and position-mediated, even though R1-32B still passes the main analysis.

On the capacity side, reducing to 384 dimensions retains 79-92% of the variance, which controls for dimensionality but not necessarily representation quality—the paper acknowledges this limitation and notes that random projections to the same dimensionality yield similar results. For the encoder-conditional advantage, HB wins 4 out of 4 times against 384-dimensional MiniLM but only 1 out of 4 against the larger BGE-large model. The paper frames this as an encoder-quality boundary, though you could argue the HS advantage partly reflects comparing against a weaker baseline. The E5-Mistral results showing 2 out of 4 wins create a monotonic gradient that actually supports the encoder-quality interpretation.

Now I'm checking the sample size consistency across the datasets. R1-32B has 100 total samples with 20 held out for testing, leaving 80 for training and validation split as 60/20. QwQ-32B has 95 total with 19 test samples, giving 76 for training and validation as 57/19. Both check out. This brings me to the critical issues I need to flag: the 32B models face severe overfitting risk with 2,240 configurations tested against only 4-10 validation samples per class, no nested cross-validation applied, and LOO-CV showing just 65-68% agreement. R1-32B only reaches significance at W=1 with 25% coverage.

The K=5 pre-selection is misleading since it was chosen on R1-8B's validation set then transferred to other models, though the K ablation across 3, 5, and 7 does stabilize the conclusions. The CR-composite classification is discovered post-hoc from the data before being used for layer selection, which the random-CP control and cosine compression help validate independently, but the discovery process needs clearer framing. Finally, R1-32B's role in the four-model claim is ambiguous—the abstract claims three of four models show confirmed HS precision gains, but R1-32B's effect is position-mediated rather than a clean confirmation.

Looking at the actual numbers, R1-32B shows only a 1.9pp gap with p=0.914 and 3.0pp selectivity below the 5pp threshold at 25% coverage, so including it in the "4/4 HB" count even with a dagger risks overstating the result. The HS advantage itself appears partially dependent on the baseline encoder choice—against 384d MiniLM it's 4/4 HB, but against 1024d BGE it drops to 1/4 HB, so the headline advantage is really contingent on which text encoder baseline is used.

But re-reading the abstract and table captions more carefully, the paper actually does say 3/4 models, not 4/4, and the evidence is properly stratified: OT-7B is strong, R1-8B is moderate with some FPR seed fragility, QwQ-32B is significant but position-competitive, and R1-32B is exploratory with position-mediated effects. The calibration here is actually quite thoughtful.

So I need to reconsider how severe these issues really are. The core question I'm wrestling with is whether the fundamental approach itself holds up.

The main contribution is methodological—showing that layer selection matters—rather than empirical, and the empirical findings are quite conditional: HS probes only outperform weak encoders at specific layers, in specific models, with substantial caveats. The paper frames itself as a characterization study rather than proposing a new method, which is honest but might limit its appeal at a top venue.

Looking at the actual numbers, the precision gains range from +15.4 to +21.9 percentage points against the 384-dimensional baseline, but only at threshold-selected layers. Against the stronger BGE-1024d encoder, only OT-7B maintains a meaningful advantage at +18.1pp. The abstract claims +19.2 to +21.9pp for three models, and checking the table, R1-8B does hit +20.1pp.

Regarding the Director's specific concerns: the statistical approach is actually quite rigorous—the Holm-Bonferroni correction is properly applied, the choice between 12 and 4 tests is transparent, and exact permutation tests serve as the primary validation despite potential issues with BCa bootstrap stability at the small sample sizes involved. The experimental design spans a 2,240-configuration search space, which raises questions about how much of the reported effect comes from selective reporting versus genuine findings.

The paper's mitigations—convergence across three independent metrics, random-CP controls, nested cross-validation for smaller models, and multi-seed stability checks—are substantial, though they don't fully resolve concerns about the 32B case. The layer selection methodology's post-hoc nature is a weakness, but independent evidence provides adequate support. The position-selectivity overlap is properly acknowledged, and R1-32B's weak residualized selectivity is transparently reported. The capacity controls using PCA dimensionality reduction and random projections are reasonable, and the encoder-quality gradient observation is noteworthy.

Now I should examine the visual presentation and figure quality before drafting the full review. I'll check the rendered PDF pages to verify the page count and visual presentation.

Wait, let me re-examine: page 8 includes Discussion section and has Figure 3. Page 9 starts the Conclusion (Section 6) and Limitations (Section 7). The page numbers are clearly visible: page 8 and page 9.

So the main text (excluding Limitations and References) includes:
- Pages 1-8: Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Method, Experiments, Discussion
- Page 9: Conclusion begins, then Limitations


Looking more closely at page 8, the Discussion section extends further with subsections on future research guidance and generalizability. The Conclusion actually starts partway through page 9, with Limitations following after that. So the main content for the page limit spans from the beginning through roughly the middle of page 9, while Limitations and References fall outside the count. The EMNLP 2026 limit is 8 pages for main text.

Since the Conclusion appears on page 9 and counts toward the main text limit, this puts the paper over the 8-page threshold. Looking more carefully at the page layout, the Discussion section spans from page 8 into page 9, with the Conclusion appearing as a brief section also on page 9, followed by Limitations. This means the main text—everything up through the Conclusion—comes to roughly 8.3 to 8.5 pages, which puts it over the 8-page limit. That's a formatting concern for the submission, though I should focus on the methodological issues instead.

Now I'm ready to structure my full review. I have what I need to write it out, starting with a summary of the paper's core contribution: the authors examine how the choice of which transformer layer to probe affects conclusions about whether hidden states or text-based approaches better detect safety commitment points in reasoning models' outputs.

The paper demonstrates that shallow-layer metrics like crossing-rate composites make hidden-state probes look ineffective, while threshold-based metrics on deeper layers reveal significant advantages—and they back this up with rigorous controls showing the bias is geometric rather than data-driven. What stands out is their methodological rigor: the five-metric ablation is well-executed, they include a random commitment-point control that independently validates their findings, and they're refreshingly honest about their results, clearly distinguishing between confirmed findings and exploratory ones. They also disclose a bug they found, which shows real transparency. The statistical framework is particularly solid, combining bootstrap confidence intervals, exact permutation tests for small samples, and multiple correction procedures across different test groupings.

They evaluate seven alternative detection methods and explain why each fails in specific ways—BOCPD struggles with gradual transitions, Mahalanobis distance misses directional signals—which prevents readers from wondering if they missed something obvious. Position residualization and capacity controls provide converging evidence that strengthens their argument.

But there's a critical concern at the 32B scale: they're searching across up to 2,240 hyperparameter configurations while their validation sets only have 4-10 samples per class, creating serious overfitting risk. mitigations for 7-8B (nested 5-fold CV showing 13-25% shrinkage, App M.1) are convincing, but explicitly infeasible for 32B ("nested cross-validation was not feasible at these sample sizes", Section 4.4). LOO-CV shows only 65-68% dominant-layer agreement (App A), and BA-optimal layers span 24 layers across folds (Table 13). The paper defers to convergence of 3 threshold-based metrics to L63 as evidence against overfitting, but this convergence is itself a single data point from a single dataset. All 32B conclusions rest on a validation set that is orders of magnitude too small for the search space. The paper acknowledges this but continues to report 32B results with the same statistical formalism (HB-corrected p-values) as the 7-8B results, risking false confidence—the † marker is easy to miss.

There's also an inconsistency around the K=5 selection: Section 2.5 claims it was "selected on the R1-8B validation set as the value balancing coverage (≥70%) and safe-trace false positive rate (≤50%)", while App I states it was "set as a design pre-selection before evaluation, not tuned on the validation set." These contradict each other. K was actually chosen based on R1-8B validation data and then applied to other models, which is a reasonable approach to avoid per-model tuning, but framing it as "pre-selection" obscures what actually happened. The K ablation (Table 9) showing stable results across K=3,5,7 helps mitigate this concern, though the inconsistent framing still undermines credibility.

The CR-composite classification also raises a garden-of-forking-paths issue. The paper admits the threshold-based category is "an empirical observation from metric disagreement, not an a priori design choice" (Section 2.4). The researchers observed that CR-composite selected shallow layers with poor results, then defined the threshold-based category which showed good results, and reported those good results. While the random-CP control (App B) and cosine compression analysis (App C) provide some independent validation, the discovery-to-confirmation loop through the same dataset is problematic. A cleaner approach would require pre-registering the layer selection criterion or testing on held-out data. The paper should be more transparent about this limitation.

The HS advantage largely reflects weak baseline choices. Against 384d MiniLM, HS wins on all 4 metrics, but against 1024d BGE-large it only wins 1/4 (Table 5, App G), and against 7B E5-Mistral just 2/4 (App I). The abstract's headline claim about "significant HS precision gains [...] +19.2 to +21.9pp" hinges entirely on which text encoder baseline is chosen. The paper discusses this encoder-quality boundary in Section 5, but the abstract foregrounds the 384d comparison without proper context, making readers think HS probes are clearly superior when the evidence actually shows this is conditional on text encoder quality. The final sentence acknowledging this conditionality doesn't adequately counterbalance the framing.

R1-32B's inclusion inflates generalizability claims. It achieves a +15.4pp precision improvement and passes HB, but the residualized gap is only +1.9pp (p=0.914), residualized selectivity is 3.0pp (below the 5pp threshold), coverage is just 25%, and significance only appears at W=1. By the paper's own standards, R1-32B's advantage is position-mediated and its safety signal is "largely positional," yet it still gets counted in statements like "all four models pass Holm-Bonferroni" with only a footnote disclaimer. This needs more prominent exclusion from count-based claims.

The GRU experiments use a different data split (70/30) compared to all other experiments (60/20/20), creating inconsistency across the evaluation.

I'm also noticing that selectivity ranges from 11.1-16.8pp while position contributes 9-20pp, with three models' selectivity values overlapping the position contribution range. The paper claims these are "orthogonal" measures, but that orthogonality claim deserves more scrutiny—if position correlates with labels (which it does at the checkpoint), then selectivity might be partially capturing position-mediated signal rather than being truly independent.

There's a page count issue here: the main text appears to extend to page 9, but EMNLP 2026 caps main text at 8 pages, which could trigger a desk rejection if it's actually over the limit.

Regarding the nested CV question—I'm wondering why reduced nested CV wasn't explored for the 32B model, even with a constrained search space like threshold-based layers and a smaller W set. That would be computationally feasible at n=95-100 and would provide more convincing evidence than LOO-CV alone.

I'm also noticing the L2-regularized logistic regression uses C=1.0 fixed, but it's unclear whether this was selected or just the default. If it's default, C should probably be included in the hyperparameter sweep; if it was selected, that's another degree of freedom that adds to the selection bias, even though Section 4.3 mentions the sweep over C ∈ [0.01, 100] shows minimal variation.

The 60/20/20 split operates at the trace level, but the metrics are computed at the step level, so I need to understand how many steps per trace and what the effective step-level sample size becomes for bootstrap. If trace lengths vary substantially, bootstrapping over traces might not adequately capture step-level variability.

For the exact permutation test in the appendix, the null assumes paired differences are symmetric around zero, but I'm not sure that assumption is actually justified.

Now I'm looking at whether one modality has systematically higher variance, which would make the sign-flip null inappropriate. The cosine compression analysis compares shallow versus deep layers, but the specific shallow layers are model-dependent—L2 for one model, L10 for another—and I need to know if these were cherry-picked to strengthen the compression narrative or if they're the actual CR-composite-selected layers. If they're cherry-picked, that's selection bias; if they're the true selected layers, the comparison is fair.

I'm also questioning why F1, AUROC, and MCC are excluded from evaluation. The justification given is that F1 conflates precision and recall, AUROC is threshold-free, and MCC is redundant with balanced accuracy, but AUROC's threshold-free property would actually be valuable for checking whether the HS advantage holds across different thresholds, especially given the layer-specific findings.

Looking at the overall assessment, the paper tackles a real methodological problem with solid rigor—the five-metric ablation, random-CP control, and statistical framework are strong. But the 32B results rely on weak validation with only 4-10 samples per class across 2,240 configurations and no nested cross-validation, the HS advantage hinges on comparing against a weak text baseline, and the post-hoc metric classification raises garden-of-forking-paths concerns. The caveats help, but the main claims are more tentative than the abstract implies. Still, there's a genuine methodological contribution here about layer selection sensitivity in safety probes.

The empirical findings are narrower than presented—the HS advantage only shows up against weak encoders, at deep layers selected retroactively, and with real statistical power only at the 7-8B scale. The paper deserves credit for its honest self-assessment and comprehensive appendix. I'm settling on a borderline conference score of 3.5, with quite high confidence after checking the statistical details carefully. The soundness sits between acceptable and strong given the rigorous framework but insufficient 32B validation and conditional HS advantage. The methodological insight is interesting but the practical scope is limited, and reproducibility is solid with thorough hyperparameter reporting.

Actually, reconsidering: the core contribution is methodological—layer selection sensitivity—which is genuinely valuable even if somewhat specialized. The empirical findings are heavily qualified. For EMNLP, 3.5 feels right as a borderline paper. The methodological rigor argues for acceptance, but the narrow scope and conditional results pull toward Findings track. The work is definitely in scope for EMNLP given the focus on reasoning model internals and safety probing methodology, and the layer selection sensitivity finding has some generalizability beyond this specific task. The encoder-quality boundary is worth noting, though the practical impact remains limited since the paper itself acknowledges these probes characterize rather than detect the phenomenon in production. I'm confident in the 3.5 score.

## Reviewer 1 — Round 1 审稿意见（方法严谨性 / 统计方法 / 实验设计）

---

## Summary

本文研究 transformer 层选择（layer selection）如何影响 hidden-state (HS) 安全探针在推理模型 chain-of-thought 中检测 safety commitment point (CP) 的结论。核心发现是方法论层面的：crossing-rate composite 指标系统性地选择浅层（32B 模型上 HS 优势消失），而 threshold-based 指标选择深层（3/4 模型显示显著 HS 优势）。论文在 4 个模型、2 个规模上评估，报告了 encoder-conditional 的 HS 优势，并提供了大量控制实验。

---

## Strengths

**[S1] 五指标层选择消融设计严谨。** CR-composite vs. threshold-based 的分歧通过 random-CP control（App B，10 次随机标签重复，100% 浅层选择确认几何偏差）和 cosine compression 分析（App C，1.4–2.7× 距离比）提供了独立验证。这不仅是一个 observation，而是一个可复现、可推广的方法论发现。

**[S2] 证据梯度（evidence gradient）的诚实分级。** 论文将自身结果分为 confirmed（OT-7B, R1-8B）、significant but position-competitive（QwQ-32B†）、exploratory（R1-32B†）三档，没有过度宣传。R1-32B 的 position mediation（residualized gap +1.9pp, p=0.914）和 bug disclosure（App K）体现了高标准的科学诚信。

**[S3] 统计框架超越 NLP 论文平均水平。** BCa bootstrap + exact sign-flip permutation test（枚举全部 2^n 排列）+ Holm-Bonferroni 两级校正（12-test 和 4-test）+ nested CV + multi-seed stability + post-hoc power analysis——这套组合在 NLP 安全领域罕见。exact permutation test 对 32B 小样本尤为必要且执行正确（App C）。

**[S4] 负面结果信息量大。** 七种替代方法（BOCPD、CUSUM、Mahalanobis、RepE、MLP、CCS、cross-model transfer）的系统性失败定义了 CP 检测的四个要求（方向性、渐进性、模型特异性、线性可分性），为后续研究提供了明确的排除清单。

**[S5] Capacity control 证据链完整。** PCA 384d（79–92% 方差保留）+ random projection 384d + 三编码器梯度（MiniLM 4/4 HB → E5-Mistral 2/4 → BGE-large 1/4）构成了收敛证据。

---

## Weaknesses

**[W1] Critical — 32B 模型超参搜索空间与验证样本严重不匹配，缺乏 nested CV**

- 具体位置：Section 2.5（评估协议）、Section 4.4（32B 分析）、App M（超参稳健性）
- 问题：搜索空间高达 2,240 配置（64 层 × 7 W × 5 K × threshold），但 32B 验证集仅 n=4–10 per class（Section 4.4："per-class validation sets contain only 4–10 traces"）。论文对 7–8B 模型执行了 nested 5-fold CV（App M.1），缩减幅度 13–25%，有效排除了超参过拟合。但对 32B 模型明确承认"nested cross-validation was not feasible at these sample sizes"（Section 4.4），LOO-CV 仅显示 65–68% dominant-layer agreement（App A），BA-optimal 层跨 fold 变化达 24 层（Table 13）。
- 为什么影响接收：这意味着所有 32B 结论（包括 Table 2 的层选择、Table 3 的 HB 通过、Section 4.3 的 position 分析）都缺乏最强的过拟合排除证据。Threshold-based 三指标收敛到 L63 是有力的间接证据，但它来自同一数据集的单次观察，不能替代交叉验证。论文使用与 7–8B 相同的统计形式（HB-corrected p 值）报告 32B 结果，† 标记容易被忽视，可能给读者虚假的信心。
- 建议：至少对缩减搜索空间（threshold-based 层 + W ∈ {1, 3, 5}）执行 nested CV；或对 32B 结果使用更保守的统计语言（如仅报告 descriptive statistics，不做推断统计结论）。

**[W2] Major — K=5 "pre-selection" 声明与正文描述矛盾**

- 具体位置：Section 2.5（"selected on the R1-8B validation set as the value balancing coverage (≥70%) and safe-trace false positive rate (≤50%)"）vs. App I（"K was set as a design pre-selection before evaluation, not tuned on the validation set"）
- 问题：这两句话直接矛盾。K 的选择确实基于 R1-8B 验证集数据，然后迁移到其他模型。这是合理的设计（固定 K 避免逐模型调参），但将其称为 "pre-selection" 不准确。
- K ablation（Table 9）显示 K=3, 5, 7 结论方向一致，这缓解了实质性担忧，但不一致的措辞损害了论文的可信度。
- 建议：统一表述为"K=5 selected on R1-8B validation and held fixed across all models"，删除 "pre-selection" 措辞。

**[W3] Major — CR-composite vs. threshold-based 分类的事后性（post-hoc）引入 garden-of-forking-paths 风险**

- 具体位置：Section 2.4（"This classification is an empirical observation from metric disagreement, not an a priori design choice"）
- 问题：研究者发现 CR-composite 选浅层（结果差）→ 定义 threshold-based 类别（结果好）→ 报告好的结果。这条发现→确认路径使用了同一数据集。Random-CP control（App B）和 cosine compression 分析提供了独立证据，但严格来说，一个 clean 的验证需要先验注册层选择准则或在 held-out 模型上验证。
- 论文在 Section 2.4 的"the ablation in Table 2 is a reproducible empirical fact independent of our framing"是合理的辩护，但应更明确标注这是事后分类（post-hoc observation），而非先验设计。
- 建议：增加一段讨论 garden-of-forking-paths 风险，明确说明 random-CP control 和 cosine compression 是独立验证而非原始发现的一部分。

**[W4] Major — HS "优势" 严重依赖弱基线，Abstract 未充分上下文化**

- 具体位置：Abstract（"+19.2 to +21.9pp, Holm-Bonferroni corrected"）、Table 3（384d vs 1024d）、App G（BGE-large）、App I（E5-Mistral）
- 问题：Against 384d MiniLM: 4/4 HB; against 1024d BGE-large: 1/4 HB（仅 OT-7B）; against E5-Mistral: 2/4 HB。标题性发现完全取决于 text encoder baseline 的选择。Abstract 前置 "+19.2 to +21.9pp"（384d 比较），最后一句 "the empirical HS advantage is conditional" 远不足以平衡。一个只看 abstract 的读者会得出"HS 探针明显优于 text monitoring"的结论，但证据表明这取决于 text encoder 质量。
- 为什么影响接收：Contribution 2（encoder-quality boundary）的价值在于揭示 HS 优势随编码器强度衰减，但 abstract 的 framing 不反映这一重要限定。
- 建议：Abstract 中在引用 +19.2–21.9pp 后立即注明 "against a 384-dimensional sentence encoder; the advantage narrows to 1/4 models against a 1024-dimensional encoder"。

**[W5] Major — R1-32B 对 count-based claims 的贡献膨胀了表观泛化性**

- 具体位置：Section 4.2（"all four models pass Holm-Bonferroni†"）、Table 3（R1-32B HB ✓）
- 问题：R1-32B 通过 HB（precision +15.4pp），但：residualized gap +1.9pp (p=0.914)；residualized selectivity 3.0pp（低于 Hewitt & Liang 2019 的 5pp 阈值）；coverage 仅 25%（5/20 traces）；仅在 W=1 显著。论文自己的标准判定其为"exploratory"且"largely positional"（Section 5）。但在 count-based claims（如 "all four models pass HB†"）中，R1-32B 与其他三个模型并列，† 标记不够显著。
- 建议：在涉及模型计数的 claim 中明确写 "three of four models"（排除 R1-32B），或使用更清晰的视觉区分（如 Table 3 中 R1-32B 行灰色背景 + 脚注说明）。

**[W6] Minor — GRU 实验使用不同数据划分**

- 具体位置：App E（"GRU experiments use a 70/30 train/test split"）、Section 2.3（"Two protocols"）
- 问题：GRU 主要使用 70/30 split，主实验使用 60/20/20。App E Table 7 提供了 R1-8B 的 60/20/20 GRU 结果，但不是所有模型都有。不同的 test set 可能包含不同的 trace 组成，使 GRU 与 LR 的跨模型比较不完全公平。
- 建议：为所有模型补充 60/20/20 GRU 结果，或在正文比较时明确标注 split 差异。

**[W7] Minor — Selectivity 与 position contribution 的数值重叠未充分讨论正交性**

- 具体位置：Section 4.2（"selectivity measures label structure [...] orthogonal to position contribution"）、App F（selectivity 11.1–16.8pp）、App K（position 9–20pp）
- 问题：论文声称 selectivity 和 position contribution 正交，但未提供形式化论证。CP 发生在 trace 的特定位置，因此 position 与 label 内在相关。Selectivity（main vs. shuffled labels）可以部分反映 position-mediated 信号，因为 shuffled labels 打破了 position-label 关联。Residualized selectivity（App F）更有信息量，但仅 R1-32B 跌至 3.0pp（低于 5pp 阈值），其余三个模型 10.4–22.9pp。
- 建议：澄清"正交"的具体含义，或改用"互补"（complementary）措辞。

**[W8] Minor — 正文页数可能超限**

- 具体位置：PDF 第 8–9 页
- 问题：从 PDF 视觉检查，Section 6（Conclusion）开始于第 9 页的上部。EMNLP 2026 正文限制 8 页（Limitations 和 References 不计）。如果 Conclusion 在第 9 页，main text 超过 8 页。
- 建议：压缩 Discussion 或 Related Work 使 Conclusion 落在第 8 页以内。

---

## Questions

**[Q1]** 为什么不在缩减搜索空间下对 32B 模型执行 nested CV？即使完整 (layer, W) 网格太大，nested CV over threshold-based 层 + W ∈ {1, 3, 5} 在 n=95–100 下可行。

**[Q2]** L2 正则化 C=1.0 是默认值还是选定的？Section 4.3 提到 C ∈ [0.01, 100] 变化 <2pp，但这次扫描本身是否算入自由度？

**[Q3]** Bootstrap 在 trace 级别操作，但指标是 step 级别。每条 trace 的步数分布如何？如果 trace 长度差异大，trace-level bootstrap 可能无法充分捕捉 step-level variability。

**[Q4]** Exact sign-flip permutation test（App C）假设配对差异围绕零对称。如果一个模态的方差系统性更高，sign-flip null 是否合适？

**[Q5]** AUROC 被排除的理由是"threshold-free and cannot diagnose the layer selection bias"（Section 2.5），但 AUROC 的 threshold-free 特性恰好可以验证 HS 优势不依赖特定阈值。排除 AUROC 是否因为它在某些层/模型上不支持 HS 优势？Table 12 补充了 AUROC（△+12.1 to +15.1pp, all p<0.01），反而支持论文结论。建议在正文提及此结果。

**[Q6]** Cosine compression 分析（Table 4）中，浅层的选择是否为 CR-composite 实际选定的层？如 R1-8B 比较的是 L2（CR-comp.）vs L14（thresh.），但 Table 2 显示 R1-8B 的 CR-composite 层也是 L14。Table 4 中 R1-8B shallow 标注为 L2 "CR-comp."，这与 Table 2 的 L14 不一致。请澄清。

---

## Missing References

未发现关键遗漏。Related Work 覆盖了 2025–2026 年的最新工作，引用密度充足。

---

## Overall Assessment

- **Overall Score: 3.5** (Borderline Conference)
- **Confidence: 4/5** (Quite sure; carefully checked statistical methodology, experimental design, and numerical claims)
- **Soundness: 3.5/5** (Between Acceptable and Strong: statistical framework rigorous, but 32B validation insufficient for the search space, and the HS advantage is more conditional than the framing suggests)
- **Excitement: 3.0/5** (Interesting: layer selection sensitivity is a genuine methodological contribution, but scope is narrow — one dataset, one attack type, limited practical impact as the paper itself acknowledges current probes are not production-ready)
- **Reproducibility: 4/5** (Mostly reproducible: hyperparameters thoroughly documented, bug disclosure shows careful record-keeping, code promised upon publication)

**简要理由：** 论文的方法论贡献（层选择敏感性）是真实且可推广的，五指标消融 + random-CP control 的设计令人信服。但实证贡献（HS 优势）高度条件化：仅对弱编码器有效（1/4 HB 对强编码器）、32B 结论缺乏 nested CV 验证（配置数/样本比 ~200:1）、R1-32B 的优势本质上是 position-mediated。Abstract 对这些条件的传达不足。论文的诚实自评和详尽附录值得肯定，但在当前状态下，empirical contribution 的窄范围和条件性使其更接近 Findings 而非主会议。

## Step 2 — 交叉回应（Reviewer 2 的完整审稿意见）

以下是 Reviewer 2 的完整审稿意见。请**逐条**回应其 Weaknesses 和 Questions：
- **[AGREE]**：同意该观点，说明理由（可补充你自己的证据）
- **[REBUT]**：反驳该观点，提供具体证据（cite 论文中的 Section/Table/Figure/Appendix）

对 Strengths 和 Missing References 也可简要评论。

---

**Reviewer 2 原文：**

### Summary
本文研究推理模型自我越狱场景下，HS 安全探针的层选择敏感性问题。使用 HarmThoughts 数据集上的四个推理 LLM，作者发现层选择指标的选择（crossing-rate composite vs. threshold-based）可以逆转 HS 探针是否优于文本探针的结论。当使用 threshold-based 层选择时，3/4 模型在 384d 文本编码器基线下显示显著 HS 精度优势；但该优势是 encoder-conditional 的（仅 1/4 在 1024d 编码器下存活），并且在 32B 规模下有模型特定的 caveats。

### Strengths
[S1] 识别了真实且被低估的方法论问题。Random-label 控制实验令人信服。
[S2] 统计分析严谨——在探针文献中是模范水平。
[S3] 诚实透明地处理 limitations。
[S4] Negative results section 信息密度高。
[S5] Encoder-quality boundary 发现有启发性。

### Weaknesses
[W1] (Critical) 核心贡献是观察性的，缺乏建设性方法论。论文刻画了问题但没有提供经验证的解决方案。五步审计工作流仅以非正式 bullet points 呈现，未在新数据/模型上验证。

[W2] (Major) 模型多样性不足：4 个模型中 3 个共享 Qwen 基座，泛化性声明（"architecture-general"浅层压缩）缺乏跨架构证据。

[W3] (Major) 单一数据集且无 IAA 报告。CP 标注模糊性可能系统性偏移层选择结论。

[W4] (Major) HS 优势被如此多的 caveats 限定（1024d 仅 1/4 HB, R1-32B position-mediated, QwQ 负 lead time, 11-50% FPR, R1-32B 仅 25% coverage），以至于实际意义不清晰。"除了'层选择要小心'之外，这篇论文提供了什么可操作的洞见？"

[W5] (Minor) Abstract framing 不对称——384d 结果前置，1024d 延后。+19.2–21.9pp 排除了 R1-32B 的 +15.4pp 但包含了 QwQ 的 +19.2pp，三个数字证据强度不均。

[W6] (Minor) Introduction framing 暗示模态比较研究，但实际贡献是方法论审计——叙事张力。

[W7] (Minor) 主文本可能轻微超页（~0.1-0.2 页）。

[W8] (Minor) 32B 结果统计功效不足但占比偏高，挤占了可用于更强贡献的篇幅。

### Questions
[Q1] 有什么跨架构证据支持浅层压缩是 architecture-general 的？
[Q2] 五步审计工作流是否在 held-out 数据/模型上验证过？
[Q3] 未来文本编码器能否完全弥合 HS-text 差距？是否有不可约 HS 优势的理论论证？
[Q4] 是否观察到 commitment 后短暂回到安全思考的 traces？
[Q5] 更强的序列模型（transformer probe）是否可能超越两种 LR 方法？

### Missing References
1. Turpin et al. (2023) unfaithful CoT
2. Azaria & Mitchell (2023) internal state lying detection
3. boxo2025linear_probes 引用真实性需确认

---

请逐条回应。特别关注你与 R2 在以下方面是否一致：
- HS 优势的实际意义（R2-W4）
- 贡献是否观察性（R2-W1）
- 模型多样性（R2-W2）
- 32B 空间分配（R2-W8）

The Director wants me to respond to Reviewer 2's review point by point, using [AGREE] or [REBUT] format, with evidence from the paper. Let me go through each item carefully.

Let me re-read my own review to check for consistency, then address each of R2's points.

Let me go through R2's weaknesses and questions one by one:

**R2-W1 (Critical): Core contribution is observational, lacks constructive methodology**
- R2 says the paper describes the problem but doesn't provide a validated solution. The 5-step audit workflow is informal.


- I partially agree here. The observation itself has real value, and the random-CP control plus cosine compression analysis go beyond pure observation by explaining the underlying mechanism. But R2 is right that we don't offer a validated solution, so I'll [AGREE] with nuance.

**R2-W2 (Major): Model diversity insufficient - 3/4 Qwen base**
- The paper actually addresses this directly in Section 5, where we acknowledge that three of the four models share the Qwen architecture and only R1-8B provides evidence from a different architecture like Llama.

**R2-W3 (Major): Single dataset, no IAA**
- The perturbation analysis in Appendix H shows the findings hold even with ±3 step shifts in the control points, which helps address concerns about annotation sensitivity. I agree it's a limitation, but the robustness check provides some reassurance. [AGREE] with caveat

**R2-W4 (Major): HS advantage has so many caveats that practical significance is unclear**
- This connects directly to my own concerns about whether the HS advantage is just an artifact of weak baselines and whether the R1-32B results are inflating our generalization claims.
- The paper itself acknowledges that the probes "characterize the commitment phenomenon rather than constitute production detectors," which means the practical utility beyond "be careful about layer selection" is pretty limited. [AGREE]

**R2-W5 (Minor): Abstract framing asymmetric**
- This matches my earlier concern. [AGREE]

**R2-W6 (Minor): Introduction framing suggests modality comparison, actual contribution is methodological audit**
- The intro poses "should a monitoring system read hidden states or generated text?" but the real finding is "layer selection can flip your answer." It's a valid observation, though I think the narrative tension is workable. [AGREE] but manageable

**R2-W7 (Minor): Page limit**
- Aligns with my earlier point about space constraints.

**R2-W8 (Minor): 32B results occupy too much space given weak statistical power**
- I see the reviewer's concern about space allocation, but the 32B analysis is actually where the layer selection sensitivity becomes most striking—the L2 versus L63 gap tells the methodological story most compellingly. The real issue isn't including 32B results, but treating them with the same statistical rigor as the 7-8B findings when they shouldn't be.
- [AGREE] partially—the per-model breakdown in Section 4.4 does take up considerable real estate for exploratory results, even though those results are essential to demonstrating the layer selection effect.

**R2 Questions:**

Q1: Cross-architecture evidence for shallow compression?
- I only have R1-8B as a second architecture point. The cosine compression pattern shows up there too (L2: 0.186 versus L14: 0.411, a 2.2× ratio), which aligns with what I'm seeing in the Qwen models, but one additional data point isn't enough to claim broad cross-architecture support.

Q2: Audit workflow validated?
- The workflow is proposed but hasn't been tested on held-out data or unseen models yet.

Q3: Can text encoders close the gap entirely?
- The paper explores encoder gradients with MiniLM-4...

Addressing the Director's specific concerns: I agree with R2 on the practical significance of the HS advantage, partially agree on the observational nature of the contribution and the space allocation to the 32B results, and agree on the model diversity limitation. I also need to track down R2's missing references, starting with Turpin et al. (2023).

Now I'm checking the references R2 flagged. Turpin et al. is an earlier work on unfaithful chain-of-thought that the paper should cite alongside chen2025unfaithful. Azaria & Mitchell (2023) on detecting deception from internal states is directly relevant to the hidden-state probing approach. The boxo2025linear_probes citation needs verification since I can't directly confirm whether it's a real reference, though it's cited in the Related Work section about linear probes relying on textual evidence.
